title: Parking Ice Cream Truck (Sliding Window Maximum)
description:
Imagine you're an ice cream truck driver in a beachside town. The beach is divided into several sections, and each section has varying numbers of beachgoers wanting ice cream given by the array of integers A.

For simplicity, let's say the beach is divided into 8 sections. One day, you note down the number of potential customers in each section: [5, 12, 3, 4, 8, 10, 2, 7]. This means there are 5 people in the first section, 12 in the second, and so on.

You can only stop your truck in B consecutive sections at a time because of parking restrictions. To maximize sales, you want to park where the most customers are clustered together.

For all B consecutive sections, identify the busiest stretch to park your ice cream truck and serve the most customers. Return an array C, where C[i] is the busiest section in each of the B consecutive sections.

NOTE: If B > length of the array, return 1 element with the max of the array.
story: Walk down the beach with a window. Keep the max of the window alive at the front of a deque — evict smaller elements from the back as you slide.
plain: You need to find the maximum element in every window of size B as you slide across the array. Use a deque (double-ended queue) to store indices of array elements in decreasing order of their values. For each new element, remove all smaller elements from the back (they can never be the max now), then add the new element. The front of the deque always holds the index of the maximum element in the current window.
tale: An ice cream vendor stands at the start of a long boardwalk divided into sections, each marked by the number of customers waiting. The vendor carries a magic notebook that remembers the busiest section in view. As the vendor slides down one section at a time, pushing a window frame that spans exactly three sections, the notebook is clever: whenever a new section enters the frame, it crosses out all older sections that are less busy than the newcomer — they can never be the answer anymore. The section written at the top of the page is always the busiest one visible through the frame.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use a deque to maintain indices of array elements in decreasing order. For each element, remove all indices from the back whose values are smaller than the current element, then add the current index. When the window is fully formed (i >= B-1), the front of the deque holds the max for that window. Before moving to the next window, remove the front if it's about to leave the window.
solutions.tale: The vendor walks the boardwalk with the magic notebook. At each step, the vendor glances at the new section entering the window. If this section is busier than the last few scribbled notes, the vendor erases those notes — they are now irrelevant. The vendor then writes the new section at the bottom. The note at the top of the page is always the busiest section currently in view. When the window slides forward, the vendor checks: is the top note about to leave the window? If yes, tear it off.
approach: Create a deque to store indices (not values) of array elements.
Iterate through the array. For each element A[i], remove all indices from the back of the deque whose corresponding values are <= A[i].
Add the current index i to the back of the deque.
If i >= B-1 (window is fully formed), the front of the deque holds the index of the max element. Record A[deque.front()] in the result.
If the front index is about to leave the window (deque.front() == i - B + 1), remove it.
Return the result array.
solutions.story: Deque maintains a decreasing sequence of potential maximums. Every new element evicts smaller ones from the back.

title: Implement Queue Using Two Stacks
description:
Implement a First In First Out (FIFO) queue using stacks only.

The implemented queue should support all the functions of a normal queue (push, peek, pop, and empty).

Implement the UserQueue class:
• void push(int X): Pushes element X to the back of the queue.
• int pop(): Removes the element from the front of the queue and returns it.
• int peek(): Returns the element at the front of the queue.
• boolean empty(): Returns true if the queue is empty, false otherwise.

NOTES:
• You must use only standard operations of a stack, which means only push to top, peek/pop from top, size, and is empty operations are valid.
• Depending on your language, the stack may not be supported natively. You may simulate a stack using a list or deque (double-ended queue) as long as you use only a stack's standard operations.
story: Two stacks: inputStack (fresh arrivals) and outputStack (ready to serve). Push goes to input. Pop/peek from output; if output is empty, flip the entire input stack into it.
plain: Use two stacks: one for pushing (input), one for popping (output). When you push, add to the input stack. When you pop or peek, take from the output stack. If the output stack is empty, transfer everything from the input stack to the output stack — this reverses the order, making FIFO work. Each element moves at most twice (once into input, once into output), so push/pop are amortized O(1).
tale: Imagine a restaurant kitchen with two counters. The left counter (inputStack) is where fresh orders arrive and pile up. The right counter (outputStack) is where the chef picks up orders to serve, always taking from the top. When the chef's counter is empty, a helper grabs the entire pile from the left counter and flips it onto the right counter. This flip reverses the order — so the oldest order, which was at the bottom of the left pile, is now on top of the right pile, ready to be served first. The restaurant serves customers in the order they arrived, using only these two counters and the rule: 'only touch the top of each pile.'

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Maintain two stacks: inputStack for new elements, outputStack for serving. Push always goes to inputStack. Pop and peek take from outputStack; if outputStack is empty, transfer all elements from inputStack to outputStack (this reverses the order). Each element is moved at most twice, making all operations amortized O(1).
solutions.tale: The helper stands between two counters. New orders always land on the left counter. When a customer asks for their food, the helper looks at the right counter. If it's empty, the helper grabs the whole left pile and flips it to the right — in one smooth motion, reversing the stack. Now the oldest order is on top of the right pile, ready to serve. The helper serves it and hands it to the customer. If the right counter already had orders, the helper just serves the top one without touching the left counter.
approach: Use two stacks: inputStack and outputStack.
push(X): Simply push X onto inputStack.
pop(): If outputStack is empty, transfer all elements from inputStack to outputStack (this reverses the order). Then pop from outputStack.
peek(): If outputStack is empty, transfer all elements from inputStack to outputStack. Then peek the top of outputStack.
empty(): Return true if both stacks are empty.
size(): Return inputStack.size() + outputStack.size().
solutions.story: One stack receives, one stack serves. Transfer only when the serving stack is empty — this flip is the key to FIFO.

title: N Integers Containing Only 1, 2, and 3
description:
Given an integer A. Find and Return first positive A integers in ascending order containing only digits 1, 2, and 3.

NOTE: All the A integers will fit in 32-bit integers.
story: BFS tree where each node spawns three children by appending 1, 2, or 3. Queue holds the frontier — generate level by level.
plain: Think of it as a tree where the root is empty, and each node has three children formed by appending 1, 2, or 3 to the parent. Use a queue to explore this tree level by level (BFS). Start with seeds 1, 2, 3 in the queue. For each number you pop, that's the next answer — then generate its three children (number*10+1, number*10+2, number*10+3) and push them to the queue. Stop after A numbers.
tale: A magician stands before three doors marked 1, 2, and 3. Behind each door is a hallway with three more doors, labeled by appending another digit — door 1 leads to 11, 12, 13; door 2 leads to 21, 22, 23; and so on. The magician opens doors one at a time, always choosing the smallest unexplored number. Each time a door opens, the magician writes the number on a scroll, then places the three child doors in a queue at the back of the line. The queue ensures the numbers are discovered in ascending order. After A doors, the scroll is complete.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Initialize a queue with 1, 2, 3. Repeat A times: pop the front element (this is the next answer), then push three new elements formed by appending 1, 2, or 3 to the popped number (multiply by 10 and add). The queue naturally maintains ascending order because smaller numbers are enqueued first.
solutions.tale: The magician puts doors 1, 2, 3 in the queue. The magician opens door 1, writes it down, and adds doors 11, 12, 13 to the back of the queue. Then opens door 2, writes it down, adds doors 21, 22, 23. Then door 3, adding 31, 32, 33. The queue now holds [11, 12, 13, 21, 22, 23, 31, 32, 33] in order. The magician continues until the scroll has A numbers.
approach: Create a queue and enqueue 1, 2, 3 (the first three valid numbers).
Create a result array of size A.
For i from 0 to A-1, dequeue the front element — this is result[i].
For the dequeued number, generate three children by appending 1, 2, 3: number*10+1, number*10+2, number*10+3.
Enqueue all three children.
Return the result array.
solutions.pseudocode:
queue = [1, 2, 3]
result = []
for i in 0..A-1:
  num = queue.dequeue()
  result[i] = num
  queue.enqueue(num * 10 + 1)
  queue.enqueue(num * 10 + 2)
  queue.enqueue(num * 10 + 3)
return result
solutions.story: BFS on an implicit tree. Each number spawns three children. Queue enforces FIFO = ascending order.

title: First Non-Repeating Character in Stream
description:
Imagine you're a teacher. You ask students to call out a letter one by one. After each letter, you jot down the very first letter that's only been called out once. If all letters have been repeated, you write "#".

Here's a scenario:

A student says "a". It's the first letter. You write "a".
Next, a student says "b", "a" is still unique, so you add "a". Now it's "aa".
A student says "a" again. Now, "b" is the unique one. You add "b", making it "aab".
A student says "b". All letters so far are repeated. You add "#". It becomes "aab#".
A student says "c". "c" is unique. You add "c". The final is "aab#c".

Your task? Given the sequence the students call out A, determine the string on the board.
story: Queue holds candidates for unique letters. HashMap tracks frequencies. After each new letter, clean the queue front until you find a unique one.
plain: Process the string character by character. Use a HashMap to track the frequency of each character, and a deque to maintain the order of characters as they first appear. For each character, increment its frequency in the map and add it to the deque if it's the first occurrence. Then, remove characters from the front of the deque while their frequency is greater than 1 (they're no longer unique). After each character, the front of the deque holds the first non-repeating character, or the deque is empty (output '#').
tale: A teacher stands before a classroom with a whiteboard and a queue of name cards. When a student calls out a letter, the teacher first checks a ledger (HashMap) to see if it's been said before. If it's new, the teacher writes the student's name card on the queue wall. Then the teacher glances at the front of the queue — the oldest name still there. If that student has spoken more than once (ledger says so), the teacher erases their name card. The teacher keeps erasing until finding a student who has spoken exactly once. That student's letter goes on the board. If no such student exists, the teacher writes '#'. The board grows one character at a time, always showing the first unique letter in the stream so far.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use a HashMap to count character frequencies and a deque to track the order of first appearances. For each character in the stream, increment its frequency and add it to the deque if it's new. Then, repeatedly remove characters from the front of the deque while their frequency is greater than 1. The front of the cleaned deque is the first non-repeating character; if the deque is empty, append '#' to the result.
solutions.tale: The teacher processes letters one by one. For each new letter, the teacher updates the ledger and adds the name card to the queue if it's fresh. Then the teacher sweeps the front of the queue, removing any cards whose owners have spoken multiple times. Whatever card remains at the front represents the first unique letter. The teacher writes it on the board. If the queue is empty, the teacher writes '#'. The board accumulates the history of first-unique letters at every step.
approach: Create a HashMap to store character frequencies and a deque to store characters in order of first appearance.
Create a StringBuilder to build the result string.
For each character in the input string, increment its frequency in the HashMap.
If it's the first occurrence (frequency becomes 1), add it to the back of the deque.
Clean the deque: while the front character has frequency > 1, remove it from the deque.
If the deque is empty, append '#' to the result. Otherwise, append the front character of the deque.
Return the result string.
solutions.story: Queue holds candidates, map filters them. Clean the queue front after every insertion.

title: Sum of Min and Max in All Subarrays
description:
Given an array A of both positive and negative integers.

Your task is to compute the sum of minimum and maximum elements of all sub-array of size B.

NOTE: Since the answer can be very large, you are required to return the sum modulo 10^9 + 7.
story: Two deques: one tracks the max (decreasing order), one tracks the min (increasing order). Slide both together, summing min+max at each window.
plain: For every subarray of size B, you need the minimum and maximum element, then sum them all up. Use two deques simultaneously: one maintains indices of elements in decreasing order (for max), the other in increasing order (for min). As you slide the window, maintain both deques by removing stale indices and elements that can't be min/max. For each fully-formed window, add the max (front of maxDeque) and min (front of minDeque) to the result.
tale: A watchman patrols a long wall with B towers visible at a time. Two scribes follow: one records the tallest tower in view (using a magic slate that erases shorter towers whenever a taller one appears), the other records the shortest tower (erasing taller ones when a shorter appears). At each step, the watchman reads both slates, adds the tallest + shortest heights, and steps forward. The slates update automatically as towers enter and leave the view. After the patrol, the watchman has the total sum of all (max + min) pairs.

solutions.label: Optimal
solutions.plain: Use two deques: maxDeque maintains indices in decreasing order of values (front = max), minDeque in increasing order (front = min). For each element, remove smaller elements from maxDeque back, remove larger elements from minDeque back. Add the current index to both. Remove indices that fall out of the window from the front of both deques. When the window is fully formed (i >= B-1), add A[maxDeque.front()] + A[minDeque.front()] to the result modulo 10^9+7.
solutions.tale: The watchman walks with two scribes. The first scribe's slate erases weaker towers as stronger ones appear, keeping the strongest on top. The second scribe's slate erases taller towers as shorter ones appear, keeping the shortest on top. Both scribes also erase the first entry if it's about to leave the window. At each window position, the watchman adds the top of both slates to the running total. The magic of the slates ensures the sum is computed in one pass.
approach: Create two deques: maxDeque (for max tracking) and minDeque (for min tracking).
Initialize sum = 0 and MOD = 10^9 + 7.
For each index i from 0 to N-1:
Remove indices from maxDeque back while A[i] >= A[back]. Remove indices from minDeque back while A[i] <= A[back].
Add i to both deques.
Remove front indices from both deques if they are < i - B + 1 (out of window).
If i >= B-1 (window fully formed), add A[maxDeque.front()] + A[minDeque.front()] to sum, modulo MOD.
Return sum.
solutions.story: Two deques, one for max, one for min. Same sliding window, different monotonic properties.
